units.title: Introductions I: Before You Start and Making Entries
units.summary: Learn what this syllabus is for, what students need before they begin, and how entries, timetables and retakes work.

p: Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language (0510) helps students understand and use English in real life. They learn to understand written and spoken English. They also learn to write and speak clearly about both familiar and less familiar topics.

Cambridge IGCSE is the most popular international qualification for 14 to 16 year olds. Students can choose from about 70 subjects. It is taught in over 4,500 schools in more than 140 countries. Universities and employers know and trust it.

b: Confident: uses a range of language to share ideas in writing and speaking.
Responsible: looks for chances to use and improve English.
Reflective: thinks about different opinions and answers politely.
Innovative: uses language in a creative way.
Engaged: tries different ways of learning and uses English in many situations.

p: Cambridge suggests that students have already studied an English as a Second Language course, such as the Cambridge Lower Secondary programme, or a national course at the same level. This is advice, not a rule.

The syllabus is planned for about 130 guided learning hours. Guided learning hours means the time a teacher spends teaching or guiding the student. Some students need fewer hours and some need more. It depends on local practice and on what the student already knows.

b: 130 hours over two school years is about 3 hours a week for 40 weeks each year.
A student who already speaks a lot of English at home may need fewer hours.
A student who is new to English may need extra lessons or extra practice at home.

sections.h: When can students take the exam?
p: Every Cambridge school belongs to one of six administrative zones. Each zone has its own timetable. You can see your timetable at www.cambridgeinternational.org/timetables.

Students can be entered in the June and November exam series. Schools in India can also enter students in the March series. Always check that you are using the syllabus for the year your students will take the exam. Private candidates can enter too, but only if the centre can run and mark the Speaking test and send the work to Cambridge for checking.

b: A school plans to teach for two years and finish in time for June. The students sit June.
A student who is not ready can wait and sit November.
A private candidate asks a school to help. The school must be able to record and assess the Speaking test first.

sections.h: Combining with other syllabuses and making entries
p: Students can take this syllabus together with other Cambridge syllabuses in the same exam series. There are a few exceptions. They cannot take it with Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language (0511) Count-in Speaking, IGCSE (9-1) English as a Second Language (0993 or 0991), IGCSE First Language English (0500), IGCSE (9-1) First Language English (0990), Cambridge O Level English Language (1123), Cambridge IGCSE English (as an Additional Language) (0472), or any syllabus with the same title at the same level.

Exams officers send the entries to Cambridge. Work closely with your exams officer so that the right students are entered for the right papers. Cambridge gives exams officers a Guide to Making Entries. It lists the entry option codes. The syllabus and all exam papers are in English only.

ex.t: Example: retakes and carrying marks forward
b: Students can retake the whole qualification as many times as they want.
Marks from Paper 3 Speaking can be carried forward to a later series. Check the Cambridge Handbook for the rules.
Students cannot send in a Speaking test from an earlier series again, in whole or in part.

units.activity: Write a one-page plan for your school. Include: how many guided learning hours you have, which exam series you will use, who your exams officer is, and the date you will talk to them about entries. Check the timetable for your zone first.

check.q: About how many guided learning hours does the syllabus plan for?
Who sends the entries to Cambridge?
In which exam series can students normally be entered?

units.title: Introductions II: Accessibility, After the Exam and Using the Grades
units.summary: Understand access arrangements, how grades and results are reported, and how teachers and students can use the grades.

sections.h: Accessibility and equality: fair for all students
p: Cambridge tries to make its syllabuses and exam papers fair for students of every country, culture and background. The language and layout of papers are planned to be as easy to access as possible. This helps all students show what they know.

Even so, some students need extra help. Cambridge uses access arrangements for students with special educational needs (SEN), a disability, an illness or an injury. These follow the idea of reasonable adjustments in the UK Equality Act (2010). They remove barriers without making the exam easier.

ex.t: Example: who might need an access arrangement?
b: A student with a hearing problem may need a different way to take the Listening test.
A student with a broken writing arm may need help with writing.
A student with a reading difficulty may need a modified paper.

p: Access arrangements must be based on evidence that the student faces a barrier. They should also match the way the student normally works at school. Cambridge must agree that the arrangement is a reasonable adjustment, has a reasonable cost and time, and does not harm the security of the exam.

Check what is available at the start of the course, not just before the exam. Read the Cambridge Handbook at www.cambridgeinternational.org/eoguide. If you need something that is not on the standard list, contact Cambridge early. A student who cannot access part of the assessment may still receive an award based on the parts they completed.

b: In week one of the course, note any students who may need help.
Collect evidence, such as notes from teachers or reports.
Ask your exams officer to check the Handbook and apply on time.

sections.h: After the exam: grades and results
p: Students receive grades A*, A, B, C, D, E, F or G. A* is the highest and G is the lowest. Ungraded means the work did not reach the standard for grade G. Ungraded appears on the statement of results but not on the certificate.

Speaking is reported separately. Where students reach the right standard, the certificate shows a Speaking grade from 1 (high) to 5 (low). The Speaking marks do not change the written grade. Sometimes the statement of results shows Q (pending) or X (no result). These letters do not appear on the certificate. The certificate names the qualification as International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE).

b: Grade B in written papers and Speaking grade 2: two separate results on one certificate.
Grade C overall with Speaking grade 2: Cambridge says this can be seen as about level B2 on the Common European Framework (CEFR).
Q means the result is pending. X means no result.

sections.h: How students and teachers can use the grades
p: Assessment has two purposes. First, it measures learning and achievement. It confirms how well a student has shown the knowledge, understanding and skills in the syllabus. Second, it shows likely future success. Results help to predict who is well prepared for a course or a job. They help students choose the best course or career.

Teachers can use results to improve teaching. Look at which skills were strong and which were weak. Ask which papers need more practice next year. Cambridge gives teachers results analysis and examiner reports for this.

ex.t: Example: using results in a staff meeting
b: Listening results were lower than Reading. Plan more listening practice.
Many students lost marks on the formal writing task. Teach register and format.
Share the examiner report with colleagues and agree two actions.

units.activity: Choose one student (or an imaginary one) and write two lines for each: (1) an access arrangement that might help and the evidence you would collect, and (2) how you would explain the student's grade and Speaking grade to the parent.

check.q: Which grade is the highest at Cambridge IGCSE?
How is Speaking reported on the certificate?
o: As part of the written grade
As a separate grade from 1 (high) to 5 (low)

check.q: When should centres check which access arrangements are available?
o: At the start of the course

units.title: Syllabus Overview: Aims, Content, Assessment and Objectives
units.summary: See the big picture: the aims, what students learn, how the three papers fit together, and the sixteen skills that earn marks.

sections.h: Aims: what the course is for
p: The aims describe the purpose of any course based on this syllabus. The aims are to: develop students' ability to use English well for practical communication; develop their awareness of the nature of language and of how to learn languages; develop skills that help in other subjects; and support their personal development and enjoyment.
Keep these four aims on your wall. When you plan a lesson, ask: will this help the student use English in real life?

b: Practical communication: students leave a voice message to book a doctor's visit.
Awareness of language: students notice how a polite email differs from a text to a friend.
Transferable skills: students plan and present a short talk they can also use in Science.
Enjoyment: students choose a topic they care about for a speaking task.

p: The course builds practical skills in reading, writing, listening and speaking. Students read many kinds of text. They learn to pick out the right details, to tell what is stated from what is only suggested, and to write for different purposes and readers.

Students listen to talks and conversations. They speak about many topics and learn to answer in a way that fits the situation and the listener, with good accuracy and clarity. By the end, they should be independent users of English for further study and for daily life.

b: Topic: protecting the environment.
Reading: an article about plastic waste.
Writing: an email to a friend about a clean-up day.
Listening: a radio interview with a volunteer.
Speaking: a short talk on how to reduce waste at home.

p: Every student takes three components and can receive grades A* to G. Paper 1 is Reading and Writing. It takes 2 hours, has 60 marks and is 70 per cent of the written grade. It has six exercises: four reading and two writing. It is marked by Cambridge.

Paper 2 is Listening. It takes about 50 minutes, has 40 marks and is 30 per cent. It has five exercises and is multiple choice. It is marked by Cambridge. Paper 3 is Speaking. It takes about 10 to 15 minutes and has 40 marks. It is an interview, a short talk and a discussion. The teacher marks it and Cambridge checks the marks. Speaking is separately endorsed: it does not change the written grade.

ex.t: Example: the numbers at a glance
b: Paper 1: 2 hours, 60 marks, 70%.
Paper 2: about 50 minutes, 40 marks, 30%.
Paper 3: about 10 to 15 minutes, 40 marks, separately endorsed (grade 1 to 5).
There are no tiers in this version of the syllabus: all students take the same papers.

p: Assessment objectives (AOs) are the skills the exam rewards. AO1 Reading: R1 understand specific facts; R2 understand how ideas, opinions and attitudes connect; R3 pick out details for a purpose; R4 understand implied meaning. AO2 Writing: W1 communicate information, ideas and opinions; W2 organise ideas with linking words; W3 use a range of grammar and vocabulary; W4 use the right register and style for the purpose and reader.

AO3 Listening: L1 specific information; L2 speakers' ideas, opinions and attitudes; L3 connections between them; L4 what is implied but not said. AO4 Speaking: S1 communicate ideas, facts and opinions; S2 control a range of vocabulary and grammar; S3 develop answers and keep talking; S4 control pronunciation and intonation. Weighting of the whole qualification: Reading 35 per cent, Writing 35 per cent, Listening 30 per cent. Speaking is separately endorsed. Inside Paper 1, Reading and Writing are 50 per cent each.

b: 'When does the festival start?' is R1 (a stated fact).
'What does the writer suggest about the town?' is R4 (implied meaning).
An informal email to a friend tests W4 (register) as well as W1 to W3.
Tell students the skill name before they practise. It helps them know what to do.

units.activity: Make a one-page poster for your classroom with the three papers (time, marks, per cent) on the left and the sixteen skills (R1 to R4, W1 to W4, L1 to L4, S1 to S4) on the right. Use your own simple words for each skill.

check.q: What share of the written grade is Paper 1 Reading and Writing?
Which objective is about understanding what is implied but not directly stated in a text?
How is Speaking (Paper 3) treated in the final result?
o: Separately endorsed with its own grade

units.title: Subject Content: Reading, Writing, Listening and Speaking
units.summary: See what students should be able to do in each skill, with clear examples and the text types they meet.

sections.h: Reading: what students learn to do
p: Students meet many kinds of text: instructions, notices, advertisements, leaflets, articles, blogs, reviews and web pages. The texts can describe, tell a story, give information, persuade, discuss or argue. Students should read widely in English, in class and at home.

They learn to find facts, to follow ideas, opinions and attitudes and the links between them, to understand what is implied, and to choose the right details for a purpose. They also learn reading strategies: skim reading (read fast to get the general idea), scanning (look for specific information) and careful reading (read slowly to understand detail). Good readers predict answers and notice what type of information a question wants.

ex.t: Example: three ways to read one blog post
b: Skim: read the title and the first line of each paragraph to learn what the post is about.
Scan: look for the date and the price when a question asks 'when' and 'how much'.
Read carefully: read the paragraph about the writer's feelings to answer an opinion question.
Guess a new word: read the sentences around it and decide what it probably means.

sections.h: Writing: what students learn to do
p: Students write for different purposes and different readers. They learn the features of each text type and are encouraged to plan, draft and check their work. They communicate facts, ideas and arguments clearly and add detail. They show control of grammar, vocabulary, punctuation and spelling.

They organise ideas in a logical order with paragraphs and linking words. For cause and effect they use words like therefore, because of, as a result and consequently. For adding ideas they use in addition, moreover and furthermore. For contrast they use however, in contrast, whereas and although. They use a range of grammar and vocabulary, such as different tenses, conditionals, phrasal verbs, collocations and idioms, and they avoid repeating the same word. They also choose the right register: informal for an email to a friend, more formal for a report, essay, review or article.

b: Informal (to a friend): 'Hi Sam! Guess what, I'm coming to your town next week. Fancy meeting up?'
Formal (to a teacher): 'Dear Mr Banda, I would like to ask whether I may hand in my essay on Friday.'
Teach students to ask: who is reading this and why am I writing?

sections.h: Listening: what students learn to do
p: Students listen to phone messages, announcements, radio programmes, TV, film, plays, news items, podcasts, conversations and interviews. These can be formal, semi-formal or informal. Students should listen to English widely in class and at home.

They learn to catch factual details such as places, names, times, dates and directions. They learn to understand speakers' ideas, feelings and attitudes, and the reasons behind them. They notice link words and pronouns. They work out what is implied and guess unknown words from the words around them. Before listening, they predict the type of information they will hear.

ex.t: Example: before, during and after listening
b: Before: read the question and decide if you need a name, a number, a place or a feeling.
During: write nothing long; listen for the key word and the link words such as but, so and because.
After: check that your answer matches what the speaker meant, not just a word you heard.

sections.h: Speaking: what students learn to do
p: Students speak in different situations: asking and answering in class, short exchanges, conversations, giving opinions and short talks. They practise functional language such as expressing preferences, telling a personal story, describing an experience, agreeing and disagreeing, giving advantages and disadvantages, and making predictions. Topics are everyday: the environment, health, food, film, travel, technology, celebrations, science, the arts and shopping.

They learn to expand answers by giving examples ('just to name a few'), giving reasons ('and that is why'), comparing ('just like', 'while'), speculating ('I suppose') and clarifying ('Sorry, I did not quite catch that'). They link ideas with discourse markers such as in addition, first of all, finally, that's why, however and although. They use a range of grammar and vocabulary and they paraphrase when they forget a word. They also work on pronunciation: word stress, sentence stress and rising and falling intonation.

b: Short: 'I like football.'
Expanded: 'I really like football, just like most of my friends. First of all, it keeps me fit, and that is why I play twice a week. However, I do not enjoy it when it rains.'
Teach students to add an example, a reason and a contrast.

p: Article: a text for a general audience, for example in a magazine or newspaper, that informs or entertains. Blog: a text published on a website, usually informal. Conversation: a spoken exchange between two or more people, usually informal. Dialogue: any spoken exchange between two people. Email: electronic writing for a particular purpose, formal or informal. Essay: a text on a topic that gives an argument or point of view, with an introduction, main body and conclusion, and reasons or examples.

Instructions: a written or spoken text that tells you how to do something. Interview: a spoken exchange in which one person asks questions and the others answer. Leaflet: an informational text that explains or advertises something and is handed out. Monologue: a text spoken by one person only. Notice: a short written text with news or information, usually put on a wall or noticeboard. Report: a text for a superior or a group about an event, experience or situation, with facts and suggestions or recommendations. Review: a text for a general audience that describes and gives opinions about something the writer has experienced.

ex.t: Example: match the need to the text type
b: You want to tell a head teacher what happened at a school trip and suggest changes: report.
You want to give your opinion on a film you saw: review.
You want to tell a friend your news in a friendly way: informal email.
You want to inform people about a school event on a wall: notice.

units.activity: Pick one topic (for example 'technology'). For that topic, write one reading task, one writing task, one listening idea and one speaking question. For each, name the text type from the glossary and the skill (R, W, L or S) it practises.

check.q: Which reading strategy means looking quickly for specific information?
Which linking word shows contrast?
A text written for a head teacher about an event, with facts and suggestions, is a:

units.title: Details of the Assessment: Paper 1, Paper 2 and Paper 3
units.summary: Walk through every exercise in the three papers: what students do, how many marks, and how Speaking is run and marked.

p: Paper 1 is a written paper. It takes 2 hours and has 60 marks. It has six exercises: four reading and two writing. Students answer every question. Students write on the question paper. Dictionaries are not allowed. Reading uses multiple-choice, matching and some short answers in English.

Exercise 1 (8 marks): read a text of about 400 to 450 words. Five questions need one answer and the last needs three. Answers are single words or phrases. Exercise 2 (9 marks): multiple matching. Read a text of about 600 to 650 words in up to five sections, or up to five shorter texts, and match nine questions to the right section. Exercise 3 (7 marks): read about 400 to 500 words and complete brief notes. Exercise 4 (6 marks): read about 550 to 600 words and answer six multiple-choice questions with three options A, B or C.

ex.t: Example: reading marks at a glance
b: Exercise 1: 8 marks. Exercise 2: 9 marks. Exercise 3: 7 marks. Exercise 4: 6 marks.
Total for reading: 30 marks.
Skills tested: R1, R2 and R3 in all four exercises, with R4 in Exercises 2 and 4.

p: Exercise 5 (15 marks) is an informal email. Exercise 6 (15 marks) is a more formal piece, such as an article, report, essay or review. In each, students write 120 to 160 words of continuous prose. They answer a short stimulus, which may include a picture, and short prompts. The stimulus tells them the purpose, format and reader, and these are different each time.

Each writing exercise is marked out of 15: up to 6 marks for Content (doing the task and developing ideas) and up to 9 marks for Language (range, accuracy and organisation). The skills tested are W1 to W4.

ex.t: Example: what to teach for the writing tasks
b: Read the task and underline the purpose, the reader and every prompt.
Plan three short points before writing.
Write 120 to 160 words: not much shorter, not much longer.
Check grammar, spelling and linking words in the last two minutes.

p: Paper 2 takes about 50 minutes, including 6 minutes to copy answers onto a separate answer sheet. It has 40 marks and 40 multiple-choice questions in five exercises. Students hear every recording twice. Check the Cambridge Handbook for the year of the exam: it explains how to get the audio and how to set up the room, equipment and sound.

Exercise 1 (8 marks): eight short extracts, one question each, with four picture options A to D. Exercise 2 (10 marks): five short extracts, two questions each, with three written options. Exercise 3 (8 marks): one monologue (for example a talk) and eight sentences to complete with a word or short phrase from three options. Exercise 4 (6 marks): six short monologues in a multiple-matching task with eight statements to choose from. Exercise 5 (8 marks): an interview between two speakers and eight multiple-choice questions.

ex.t: Example: listening marks at a glance
b: Exercise 1: 8. Exercise 2: 10. Exercise 3: 8. Exercise 4: 6. Exercise 5: 8.
Total: 40 marks.
Skills tested: L1, L2 and L3 in all exercises, and L4 in Exercises 2, 4 and 5.

p: The Speaking test is about 10 to 15 minutes and is worth 40 marks. It is in English and must be recorded in full for every student. Dictionaries are not allowed. The teacher or examiner chooses one Speaking Assessment card for each student. The teacher conducts and marks the test, and Cambridge checks (moderates) the marks.

The test has five parts. Introduction (about 1 minute): start the recording, say your name, the student's number and name and the date, welcome the student and read the script. Not assessed. Warm-up (1 to 2 minutes): a short friendly chat. Not assessed. Part 1 Interview (2 to 3 minutes): a short interview on a topic. Assessed. Part 2 Short talk (3 to 4 minutes, with 1 minute to prepare): the student reads the card, prepares without writing notes, then talks alone. Assessed. Part 3 Discussion (3 to 4 minutes): questions linked to the Part 2 topic. Assessed.

b: Introduction and warm-up put the student at ease. They earn no marks.
Interview, short talk and discussion are the three assessed parts.
The student receives a card only for Part 2. The questions for Parts 1 and 3 are in the teacher's notes.
The whole test, from the start of the introduction to the end of Part 3, must be recorded.

sections.h: Marking Speaking, moderation and sending marks
p: Speaking is marked out of 40 on four criteria, each out of 10: grammar, vocabulary, development and pronunciation. Add the four marks for the total. The marks come from level descriptions from Level 5 (9 to 10 marks) down to Level 1 (1 to 2 marks), with 0 for no creditable response. Choose the best-fit level first. If the work convincingly meets the level, give the top mark. If it adequately meets it, give a middle mark. If it only just meets it, give the lowest mark.

Record marks on the Speaking Examination Summary Form, which you download each year from the samples database at www.cambridgeinternational.org/samples. The marks on the form must be the same as the marks you send. If more than one teacher marks Speaking in your school, you must standardise (internally moderate) the marking so that every student is judged to the same standard. Cambridge then externally moderates: you send the marks of all students and a sample of the marked work. Moderators write a short report with feedback for your centre.

b: Level 5: answers are relevant and consistently well developed; the student keeps talking with ease.
Level 4: answers are relevant and mostly developed; the student keeps talking with only a little support.
Level 3: answers are relevant with attempts at development; frequent support is needed.
Use the descriptors, not your feeling, to decide.

How many times do students hear each recording in Paper 2?
o: As many times as they ask

units.title: Assessing the Syllabus: How Marks Are Awarded
units.summary: Learn the six marking principles examiners follow, and how to read a mark scheme so you mark the same way Cambridge does.

sections.h: Why teachers need the mark scheme
p: A mark scheme shows how examiners were told to give marks. It is published to help teachers and students understand what the exam asks for. It does not show every discussion examiners had about other acceptable answers, so read it together with the question paper and the Principal Examiner's Report for Teachers.

In this week you will use real June 2024 papers: Paper 1 (0510/11) and Paper 2 (0510/21). You will learn to mark like an examiner. Then you will use the same skills to give better feedback to your students.

b: Question paper: shows what students must do.
Mark scheme: shows which answers earn marks.
Examiner's report: explains what students did well and badly and gives advice for next time.

p: Principle 1: marks follow the mark scheme or level descriptors, the skills named in them, and the standard shown in the standardisation scripts. Principle 2: marks are always whole marks. There are no half marks.

Principle 3: marks are given positively. Examiners give marks for correct and valid answers, and for what students clearly show they know and can do. Marks are not taken away for errors or for leaving things out. Spelling, punctuation and grammar are judged only where the question tests them, but the meaning must always be clear.

Principle 4: rules are used the same way for every script. Principle 5: use the full range of marks when students' work deserves it. Principle 6: marks come only from the mark scheme. Do not think about grade boundaries or grade descriptions while marking.

b: A student writes 'sharing a car' where the key says 'sharing a car': mark given.
A student's English has small spelling mistakes in a short answer but the meaning is clear: mark still given.
A student leaves one bullet empty: no mark for that bullet, but no mark is taken from the other bullets.

p: For short-answer questions, a word or phrase in brackets ( ) may be written but is not needed. For example the key for Question 1 is '(19)84'. A student who writes '84' or '1984' gets the mark. Where the key shows a slash, such as 'taking photographs / selling photographs / charge for photographs', any one of these ideas earns the mark.

For questions with several marks, the key often says 'award one mark for each detail up to a maximum of three marks.' This means a student cannot score more than three, even if they write five correct things. For multiple-choice and matching questions, there is one correct letter.

ex.t: Example: what the notes in a key mean
b: Brackets ( ): can be included, not essential.
Slash /: alternative acceptable answers.
'Up to a maximum of 4 marks': stop counting at four.
'Award one mark for each detail': mark each idea separately.

sections.h: Level descriptors and best fit (for writing and speaking)
p: Writing is marked with level descriptors, not a list of answers. First read the whole script. Then decide which level statement is the best fit. Real work does not always match one level exactly, so you may need to choose between two levels.

Then choose the mark inside the level. If the work convincingly meets the level, give the top mark. If it adequately meets the level, give a middle mark. If it only just meets the level, give the lowest mark.

ex.t: Example: choosing a mark inside a level
b: Language level 4 to 6 means 'generally good'. A script with a good range and few errors: 6.
A script that meets the level adequately: 5.
A script that only just reaches the level: 4.

units.activity: Print the first page of the June 2024 mark scheme for Paper 1 (0510/11). Highlight the six generic principles in six colours. Then write one sentence for each principle that tells a new colleague what it means in a classroom marking session.

check.q: What does a mark scheme tell you?
o: How examiners were told to give marks
How long to teach each topic

check.q: A key says: 'Award one mark for each detail up to a maximum of three marks.' A student gives four correct details. What is the mark?
Which statement matches positive marking?
o: Every spelling mistake loses a mark
Marks are not taken away for errors or omissions

units.title: Marking Exercise 1 and Exercise 3: Short Answers and Notes
units.summary: Use the June 2024 cosplay blog and the car-free cities article to practise marking short answers and note-making.

p: In June 2024 Exercise 1 was a blog by a teenager called Lana about her hobby, cosplay. Cosplay means dressing up as a character from a film, book or video game. There are five one-mark questions and one three-mark question. Students write a word or a short phrase.

Look at the answers. Question 1 asks when the word cosplay was invented. The blog says the activity began in 1939 but the name was created in 1984, so the answer is (19)84. A student who writes 1939 is answering a different question. Question 2 asks what type of cosplay Lana prefers. She says she likes science fiction but she would choose fantasy before anything else, so the answer is fantasy.

b: Q1 When was the term invented? (19)84.
Q2 What type of cosplay does Lana prefer? fantasy.
Q3 Most famous cosplay contest? World Cosplay Summit.
Q4 What is she planning to be next? non-human role or character.
Q5 How would she like to make money? taking, selling or charging for photographs.
Q6 Three benefits (1 mark each, up to 3): many friends; gained confidence; more creative; learned to sew.

p: Many wrong answers come from reading too fast. In Question 1, 1939 and 1984 are both in the text. In Question 2, science fiction and fantasy are both in the text. The student has found a real fact, but not the right one. Teach students to underline the question word (when, what type, how) and to match the answer to it.

In Question 6, a student may write 'she has made friends and gained confidence and become more creative and learned to sew and she is proud'. Only three marks are available, so do not count past three. Teach students to write the three clearest details and then stop.

b: Q1 'it started in 1939': 0 marks. The name was created in 1984.
Q2 'science fiction': 0 marks. She likes it but prefers fantasy.
Q5 'selling costumes': 0 marks. She says she cannot imagine selling hers.
Q6 'more friends, confidence, creative': 3 marks.

sections.h: Exercise 3: the car-free cities notes (7 marks)
p: Exercise 3 asks students to read a 400 to 500 word article and fill in short notes under headings. In June 2024 the article was 'Car-free cities'. The task: imagine you are giving a talk to classmates about reducing car use in cities. Question 8 asks for four policies that have been introduced. Question 9 asks for three things the writer tried to reduce his own car use.

The key for Question 8 lists five acceptable answers: removing parking places, car-free zones, charging drivers to enter parts of a city, better public transport, and parking charges outside the workplace. Any four earn the four marks. The key for Question 9 lists renting an e-bike or bike, sharing a car, making a personal travel plan or getting personalised advice, and downloading an app. Any three earn three marks.

b: Use words from the article. You do not have to use full sentences.
Keep each note short: a few words is enough.
Match the heading. Policies in Question 8, the writer's own actions in Question 9.
Do not repeat the same idea twice. 'Car-free zones' and 'zones without cars' count as one answer.

sections.h: Marking practice: is the answer in the right place?
p: In Exercise 3 an answer must belong under the right heading. For example, 'renting an e-bike' is something the writer tried himself, so it belongs in Question 9. If a student writes it as a policy in Question 8, it does not earn a mark there.

Another trap is copying too much. If a student copies a whole sentence that includes the correct idea together with wrong information, the answer can lose the mark, because it is no longer clear and accurate. Teach students to cut the answer down to the key words.

b: Q8 'removing parking places': 1 mark.
Q8 'renting an e-bike': 0 marks. This is the writer's own action, not a policy.
Q9 'sharing a car': 1 mark.
Q9 'London reduced traffic by 33 per cent': 0 marks. It is a result, not what the writer tried.

units.activity: Take Exercise 1 and Exercise 3 from the June 2024 Paper 1 question paper in the download pack. Write the questions on a sheet and ask a colleague (or a student) to answer them. Then mark their answers using the mark scheme and write one feedback sentence for every lost mark.

check.q: Question 1 asks when the word 'cosplay' was invented. Which answer earns the mark?
The key for Question 8 gives five policies but the question has four marks. How many marks can a student score?
A student writes 'renting an e-bike' as a policy in Question 8. What is the mark?
o: 0, because it is the writer's own action, not a policy

units.title: Marking Exercise 2 and Exercise 4: Matching and Multiple Choice
units.summary: Practise matching statements to people (wild swimming) and multiple-choice reading (ToddlerLab) and learn to teach evidence-based answers.

p: Exercise 2 is a matching task. In June 2024 students read an article with four people, A Conor, B Emine, C Omar and D Ana, who enjoy wild swimming. Wild swimming means swimming outdoors in rivers, lakes and the sea. There were nine statements, 7(a) to 7(i). Students write the letter of the person each statement matches. Each is worth one mark.
The key is: (a) C, (b) B, (c) A, (d) D, (e) A, (f) D, (g) C, (h) B, (i) D. Notice that A, B, C and D are each used more than once. This is why students must find the idea, not just a matching word.

ex.t: Example: why each answer is right
b: (a) Better than a pool: Omar prefers fresh air to chemicals (C).
(b) Why they do not say where they swim: Emine says regular swimmers value private places (B).
(c) Prefers to go alone: Conor enjoys the times he has only himself for company (A).
(d) Surprised by wildlife: Ana saw a seal next to her and did not expect it (D).

sections.h: More Exercise 2 answers: the hard ones
p: (e) 'describes the effect on their state of mind' is A: Conor says he comes out feeling more positive than when he went in. (f) 'will go whatever the weather' is D: Ana says it does not matter how cold or wet it is. (g) 'a memory might have been inaccurate' is C: Omar says he had to be reminded of a worry he forgot, so his memory was incomplete.

(h) 'gives advice for newcomers' is B: Emine says to get into the water slowly and warm up quickly afterwards. (i) 'done something risky' is D: Ana goes in alone even though she knows it is not a good idea. These statements test R2 and R4: students must see the meaning behind the words, not only the same words.

ex.t: Example: teaching tip, the evidence line
b: For every answer, students underline the exact words in the text that prove it.
Then they write the letter.
If two texts seem to fit, they ask: which one is the best match for the whole statement?
This habit stops lucky guessing.

p: Exercise 4 has a longer article (550 to 600 words) and six multiple-choice questions with options A, B or C. In June 2024 the article was about ToddlerLab, a research laboratory at the University of London where scientists study how young children's brains develop. Questions 10 to 15 test main ideas, details, attitudes and the meaning of a phrase.

The key is: Q10 B, Q11 C, Q12 C, Q13 B, Q14 A, Q15 B. Q10 asks why Serena is interesting: because she wears a special cap with wires. Q11 asks what the second paragraph says: why it has been harder to study young children's brains than babies' brains. Q12 asks why she wears gloves: so cameras can record her hand movements. Q13: she begins her house-building task by watching a short video.

b: Q14 is A: the house-building task shows how young children follow instructions (the article says three-year-olds struggle with complex commands).
Q15 is B: 'as she does so' refers to Serena running around the room, which means moving rapidly.
Reference words such as 'so', 'this' and 'it' point back to an earlier idea. Teach students to look back one sentence.

sections.h: Marking and teaching with multiple choice
p: Multiple-choice marking is easy: one correct letter, one mark. Your teaching work is harder. A wrong option is called a distractor. Distractors often use words from the text but give a different meaning. For example, in Question 10 option A says 'unusually clever'. The article says there is nothing special about Serena except the cap, so A is wrong.

After a practice test, do not only say 'the answer is B'. Ask students to show the line in the text that proves B and the line that proves why A and C are wrong. This is how students learn the skill, not just the answer.

b: Give back the paper without marks.
Students find the evidence for each answer in pairs.
Check together with the key.
Students write one 'next time I will...' sentence about their biggest mistake.

units.activity: Choose Exercise 2 from the June 2024 paper. Cover the key. For each statement (a) to (i), write the letter AND the exact words from the text that prove it. Then check against the key. Count how many of your evidence lines you could quote.

check.q: In the June 2024 wild swimming task, which person says they prefer swimming alone (statement c)?
What is a distractor in a multiple-choice question?
o: A wrong option that looks attractive

check.q: In ToddlerLab Question 12, why is Serena asked to wear gloves?
o: To make her fingers more visible
So the cameras can record her movements

units.title: Marking Exercise 5 and Exercise 6: Writing with the Mark Scheme
units.summary: Learn the Content and Language tables, mark a sample email step by step, and plan a good review.

sections.h: The two writing tasks of June 2024
p: Exercise 5 (Question 16, 15 marks) asked for an informal email to a friend. The situation: you have decided to help at a sports event in your town next month. The email had to describe the event, say why you decided to help and explain what you will be doing, in about 120 to 160 words. A picture of a woman in sports clothes holding a folder was given.

Exercise 6 (Question 17, 15 marks) asked for a review of a new magazine for teenagers, to be posted on the school website. Four speech bubbles gave ideas: it is quite expensive; I would prefer longer articles; there are some interesting topics; I love the photos. Students could use these ideas and should add ideas of their own. Both tasks are marked with the same two tables: Table A Content (up to 6) and Table B Language (up to 9).

ex.t: Example: what is the same and what is different
b: Same: 120 to 160 words, 6 marks for Content, 9 for Language.
Different: Exercise 5 is informal (to a friend). Exercise 6 is more formal (a review for a school website).
Teach students to read: purpose, reader, format, prompts.

p: Content has two parts: task fulfilment and development of ideas. At 5 to 6 marks, the task is fulfilled, the content is fully relevant throughout, the style is consistently right for the text type, there is an excellent sense of purpose and audience, and ideas are very well developed. At 3 to 4 marks, each of these is 'generally' true. At 1 to 2 marks, the task is only partly fulfilled, content is only partly relevant, style is inconsistent or wrong, and there is only a limited attempt to develop ideas. 0 means no creditable response.
In simple words: did the student do what the task asked, for the right reader, in the right style, and did they explain their ideas with details?

b: Did the student cover every bullet or prompt?
Is everything relevant to the task?
Is the style right for a friend (informal) or a website review (more formal)?
Are there details, reasons or examples, not just one line per bullet?

p: Language also has two parts: range and accuracy, and organisation. At 7 to 9 marks, content is communicated skilfully, with a wide range of common and less common vocabulary, a wide range of simple and complex structures, a high level of accuracy (occasional errors do not impede communication), effective organisation and a wide range of linking words.

At 4 to 6 marks, content is communicated clearly, with a range of common vocabulary and attempts at less common words, a range of simple structures and attempts at complex ones, a generally good level of accuracy and a range of linking words used generally appropriately. At 1 to 3 marks, content lacks clarity, only common vocabulary and simple structures are used, and errors impede communication, with a limited attempt at organisation and linking.

b: Vocabulary: only common words, or some less common words too?
Structures: only simple sentences, or some complex sentences (because, although, if)?
Accuracy: do errors stop you understanding?
Organisation: paragraphs, clear order, linking words such as also, because, however?

p: Read this sample answer to Question 16 (written for this course, not a Cambridge script, about 130 words): 'Hi Sam, How are you? I have some good news to tell you. Next month there is a big running race in our town and I decided to help there as a volunteer. The race is for everyone, children and adults, and about 500 people will take part. It start at the town park at nine o'clock and finish near the market. I decided to help because I love sport and I want to do something good for my town. Also, my teacher said it will be a good experience for my CV. I will be giving water to the runners and I will help to show them the way. I will also say well done to them at the end. Would you like to come and help with me? It would be more fun together! Write soon, Tolu'.

Marking: Content. All three bullets are covered, ideas are developed with some detail, and the informal style is right. Content: 5 out of 6. Language. Content is communicated clearly, with simple structures used well and some complex ones (because, I decided to...). Errors such as 'It start' and 'finish' are small and do not impede meaning. Vocabulary is mostly common. Linking words (also, because) are used generally appropriately. Language: 5 out of 9. Total: about 10 out of 15. Different markers may differ by one mark; the important thing is to use the table to explain your decision.

ex.t: Example: how to lift this script
b: Add a wider range of vocabulary (for example, 'cheer them on', 'a great opportunity').
Use more complex structures (for example, 'If the weather is good, I will ...').
Check agreement: 'It starts ... and finishes ...'.
Add a little more detail to the reason for helping.

units.activity: Write your own 120 to 160 word answer to the June 2024 magazine review (Question 17) using at least two of the speech-bubble ideas and one idea of your own. Then mark it with Tables A and B: write the Content mark, the Language mark, and one sentence of evidence for each.

check.q: How many marks are available for Content in each writing task?
Which Language band says 'content is communicated clearly' with a 'generally good' level of accuracy?
What should you do first when marking a writing script?
o: Read the whole script and decide which level fits best
Give the top mark in the level

units.title: Paper 2 Listening, Past Papers and the Examiner's Report
units.summary: Learn how to use the June 2024 Listening paper and mark scheme, how to run a past-paper lesson, and how to use an examiner's report to improve your teaching.

sections.h: Paper 2 Listening: the shape of the paper
p: Paper 2 has 40 multiple-choice questions in five exercises and takes about 50 minutes, including 6 minutes to copy answers onto a separate answer sheet. Every recording is played twice. The June 2024 paper (0510/21) has audio, a mark scheme and a transcript.

Exercise 1 (Q1 to Q8): eight short extracts with four picture options A to D. Exercise 2 (Q9 to Q18): five short extracts, two questions each, with three options. Exercise 3 (Q19 to Q26): one talk, complete eight sentences with three options. Exercise 4 (Q27 to Q32): six short monologues, match each to one of eight statements (A to H). Exercise 5 (Q33 to Q40): an interview, eight questions with three options.

b: Exercise 1: 8 marks. Exercise 2: 10 marks. Exercise 3: 8 marks. Exercise 4: 6 marks. Exercise 5: 8 marks.
Total: 40 marks.
Where to check the audio: Cambridge Handbook, www.cambridgeinternational.org/eoguide.

p: Questions 1 to 8: A, C, C, B, D, C, D, A. Questions 9 to 18: C, B, B, C, A, A, C, B, A, B. Questions 19 to 26: C, A, B, A, C, B, A, C.

Questions 27 to 32 (matching): G, A, F, B, C, H. Questions 33 to 40: C, B, B, A, C, A, C, B. Each correct answer earns one mark and there are no half marks. Keep a copy of the transcript beside the key so you can show students the exact words that prove each answer.

ex.t: Example: mark and analyse in 20 minutes
b: Give each student the answer key to self-mark in a different colour pen.
Make a table of the five exercises and ask students to count marks per exercise.
Find the exercise with the lowest total across the class: that is the next lesson.
Replay one extract with the transcript and underline the key words.

p: A good past-paper lesson has four steps. Step 1, predict: before listening or reading, students look at the questions and guess the type of answer needed (a name, a number, a feeling). Step 2, do it under test conditions with the real timing. Step 3, mark with the mark scheme. Step 4, learn: talk about why wrong answers were wrong.

Do not use every past paper as a test. Use some as practice for one skill only. For example, use only Exercise 3 of Paper 2 for a short 10-minute listening practice at the start of a lesson. This gives students many chances to practise without tiring them.

ex.t: Example: one week plan with past papers
b: Monday: Paper 1 Exercise 2 (matching), 20 minutes, mark together.
Wednesday: Paper 2 Exercise 4 (monologues), play twice, then discuss clues.
Friday: Paper 1 Exercise 5 (email), write in 25 minutes, peer-mark with Table A and Table B.

p: The Principal Examiner's Report for Teachers is published for each exam series on the Cambridge website. It tells you how students answered each question, what the best answers did, what went wrong, and what to teach next. Read it with the question paper and the mark scheme open. For each question ask: what was the common mistake, and what could I do in my next lesson to avoid it?

Use the report to plan, not just to read. Make a one-page action list: three things students did well, three things to change in your teaching, and the exercise you will practise first next term. Share the page with your department.

ex.t: Example: turning a report into action
b: Report says: students copy long sentences in short-answer questions. Action: teach 'cut to the key words' in two lessons.
Report says: students match words, not ideas. Action: do the 'evidence line' routine.
Report says: writing is too short. Action: practise adding reasons and examples.

p: In the download pack for this course you will find: the June 2024 Paper 1 question paper and mark scheme, the June 2024 Paper 2 mark scheme, and the Paper 2 audio (MP3). Cambridge also publishes the Paper 2 question paper, the transcript and the examiner's report on its website for teachers.

Always check that you have the paper for the right year and the right paper number (0510/11 for Reading and Writing, 0510/21 for Listening). Keep your own copy of each mark scheme and write notes on it after each lesson.

b: Question paper 0510/11 June 2024.
Mark scheme 0510/11 June 2024.
Mark scheme 0510/21 June 2024.
Audio for Paper 2 (MP3) and the transcript from Cambridge.

units.activity: Create a one-page Past Paper Plan for the next four weeks. For each week write: the paper and exercise, the skill being practised (R1 to R4, W1 to W4, L1 to L4), how you will mark it, and one feedback action. Then read the June 2024 examiner's report for Paper 1 and add two actions that come from it.

check.q: How many times is each recording played in Paper 2 Listening?
In the June 2024 Listening mark scheme, what is the answer to Question 27?
What is the best way to use the examiner's report?
o: Read it once and forget it
Use it only to find grade boundaries
Give it to students without discussion
Make an action list for your next lessons

questions.q: About how many guided learning hours is the 0510 syllabus planned for?
questions.why: The syllabus is designed around about 130 guided learning hours, but this is only guidance.

questions.q: What does 'guided learning hours' mean?
o: Time spent in the exam hall only
Time a student spends on holiday
Time a teacher spends teaching or guiding the student
questions.why: It is the time a teacher spends teaching or guiding students.

questions.q: In which exam series can students normally be entered?
questions.why: Students can be entered in June and November. Schools in India can also use March.

questions.q: Which extra series is open to schools in India?
questions.why: Schools in India can also enter candidates in the March series.

questions.q: Who sends the entries to Cambridge International?
questions.why: Exams officers are responsible for submitting entries.

questions.q: Why do Cambridge schools have an administrative zone?
o: Each zone has its own exam timetable and papers
questions.why: Papers and timetables are produced for different zones to keep exams secure.

questions.q: Which of these can a student take together with 0510 in the same series?
questions.why: Different subjects can be combined. The English-language syllabuses listed as exceptions cannot.

questions.q: Can students retake the qualification?
o: Only if they got grade G
Yes, as many times as they want
questions.why: Candidates can retake the whole qualification as many times as they want.

questions.q: What is true about Speaking tests from an earlier series?
o: They cannot be sent in again, in whole or in part
Only the interview can be reused
They can always be sent in again
They are deleted by Cambridge after one day
questions.why: Candidates cannot resubmit Speaking tests from a previous series.

questions.q: In which language are the syllabus and assessment materials available?
questions.why: This syllabus and its assessment materials are available in English only.

questions.q: What is an access arrangement?
o: A way to make the exam easier for everyone
A change that removes a barrier for a student with SEN, disability, illness or injury
questions.why: Access arrangements are reasonable adjustments that remove barriers without lowering the standard.

questions.q: When should a centre check which access arrangements are available?
o: At the start of the course
questions.why: Availability should be checked at the start of the course.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a condition for approving an access arrangement?
o: It makes the exam easier for the student
It has a reasonable cost and timeframe
It does not harm the security of the assessment
questions.why: Arrangements must be reasonable and must not weaken the exam. They are not meant to make it easier.

questions.q: What does the grade 'Ungraded' mean?
o: The work did not reach the standard for grade G
questions.why: Ungraded means the standard for grade G was not reached.

questions.q: Which letter on a statement of results means 'pending'?
questions.why: Q means pending. X means no result.

questions.q: How is Speaking reported where students reach the right standard?
o: With the letters Q or X
Inside the A* to G grade
questions.why: Speaking is separately endorsed with grades 1 to 5.

questions.q: Cambridge says grade C overall with Speaking grade 2 can be seen as roughly which CEFR level?
questions.why: The syllabus states this combination can be considered equivalent to B2.

questions.q: How long is Paper 1 Reading and Writing and how many marks does it have?
questions.why: Paper 1 is 2 hours and 60 marks.

questions.q: What share of the written grade is Paper 2 Listening?
questions.why: Listening is 30 per cent. Paper 1 is 70 per cent.

questions.q: Which statement about Paper 3 Speaking is correct?
o: It is marked only by Cambridge examiners
It is internally assessed and externally moderated
It is part of the written grade
questions.why: The teacher marks Speaking and Cambridge moderates the marks.

questions.q: Which assessment objective is about understanding implied meaning in reading?
questions.why: R4 is understanding implied meaning.

questions.q: Which writing objective is about the right register and style for the purpose and reader?
questions.why: W4 covers register and style.

questions.q: Reading quickly to get the general idea of a text is called:
questions.why: Skim reading means reading fast for the general idea.

questions.q: Which word shows contrast?
questions.why: Although, however, whereas and in contrast show contrast.

questions.q: Which text type is usually informal and published on a website?
questions.why: A blog is usually informal and published online.

questions.q: How many exercises are in Paper 1?
o: Six: four reading and two writing
Four: two reading and two writing
questions.why: Paper 1 has four reading and two writing exercises.

questions.q: How are the 15 marks for each writing exercise shared?
questions.why: Up to 6 for Content and up to 9 for Language.

questions.q: How many times do students hear each recording in Paper 2?
questions.why: Candidates hear each recording twice.

questions.q: In the Speaking test, which parts are assessed?
questions.why: Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3 are assessed. The introduction and warm-up are not.

questions.q: How is the Speaking test marked?
o: Four criteria (grammar, vocabulary, development, pronunciation) each out of 10
questions.why: Each of the four criteria has a maximum of 10 marks, giving 40 in total.

questions.q: Which statement matches the Cambridge marking principle about errors?
o: Marks depend on the student's grade target
Marks are not deducted for errors or omissions
Half marks may be given for small errors
Marks are deducted for every error
questions.why: Principle 3: marks are awarded positively and are not taken away for errors or omissions.

questions.q: Can an examiner give a half mark?
o: No, marks are always whole marks
questions.why: Principle 2: marks are always whole marks.

questions.q: In a mark scheme, text in brackets ( ) means the text:
o: may be included but is not essential
is worth a mark by itself
questions.why: The mark scheme says bracketed text may be included but is not essential.

questions.q: When marking with a level descriptor, work convincingly meets the level. Which mark do you give?
o: The lowest mark in the level
The highest mark in the level
questions.why: Convincingly meets the level means the top mark. Adequately means a middle mark. Just meets means the lowest mark.

questions.q: Why should examiners not think about grade thresholds while marking?
o: Marks are based only on the mark scheme requirements
questions.why: Principle 6: marks are based solely on the requirements in the mark scheme.

questions.q: In June 2024 Exercise 1, which answer earns the mark for 'When was the term cosplay invented?'
questions.why: The text says the activity started in 1939 but the name was created in 1984.

questions.q: What type of cosplay does Lana prefer?
questions.why: She likes science fiction but says fantasy is what she would choose first.

questions.q: Question 6 asks for three details and has three marks. A student writes five correct details. How many marks?
questions.why: The key says up to a maximum of three marks.

questions.q: Which of these is a POLICY introduced to reduce car use in the June 2024 article?
questions.why: Car-free zones is a policy. The other three are things the writer tried himself.

questions.q: Which answer is acceptable for Question 9, what the writer tried to reduce his own car use?
o: charging drivers to enter the city
questions.why: Sharing a car is something the writer did himself. The others are policies.

questions.q: How many marks are there in Exercise 3 (Questions 8 and 9)?
questions.why: Question 8 is 4 marks and Question 9 is 3 marks, so 7 in total.

questions.q: In the June 2024 wild swimming task, who is the best match for 'explains why they avoid saying where they swim' (7b)?
questions.why: Emine says regular swimmers value their private places.

questions.q: Who is the best match for 'mentions being surprised to see wildlife while swimming' (7d)?
questions.why: Ana describes a seal appearing next to her and says she did not expect it.

questions.q: Who is the best match for 'will go wild swimming whatever the weather' (7f)?
questions.why: Ana says it does not matter how cold or wet it is.

questions.q: In ToddlerLab, why is Serena asked to wear special gloves (Question 12)?
o: So cameras can record her hand movements
To make her fingers easier to see
questions.why: The gloves have reflective material so ceiling cameras can follow her hands.

questions.q: What does 'as she does so' refer to in ToddlerLab Question 15?
questions.why: It refers to running around the room, which is moving rapidly.

questions.q: How are the 15 marks shared in Paper 1 Exercises 5 and 6?
o: Up to 6 for Content and up to 9 for Language
Up to 9 for Content and up to 6 for Language
questions.why: Table A Content is up to 6 and Table B Language is up to 9.

questions.q: What does the Content table assess?
o: Task fulfilment and development of ideas
questions.why: Content covers task fulfilment (relevance, style, purpose and audience) and development of ideas.

questions.q: How many questions are there in Paper 2 Listening and how many marks?
questions.why: Paper 2 has 40 multiple-choice questions, each worth one mark.

questions.q: In the June 2024 Listening key, what is the answer to Question 27?
questions.why: Question 27 is in the multiple-matching exercise (Exercise 4) and the key gives G.
